issues.legal_issue: A municipal authority may adopt an unconventional private-developer financing and execution model for a project when the model is within its powers and does not violate legal or constitutional limits or amount to a clear abuse of power.
material_facts: The Municipal Council sought to put municipal land to a more useful and profitable use by constructing administrative, market and commercial facilities.

The project was to be financed and executed at the developer’s expense; the Council was to receive its administrative building without cost, while the developer could retain premiums from occupancy rights in the remaining commercial accommodation to meet the project’s costs and profit.
The Council’s financial commitments made it difficult to provide the project’s required funds itself.
The project was challenged as an impermissible and arbitrary policy choice, but the Court found it within the Council’s powers.
issues.conclusion: The project was not invalid merely because the Council used an unconventional method of financing and execution, and there was no basis to quash the Council’s resolution on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 14 and 298 of the Constitution, economic and administrative policy choices are generally for the authority to make. Judicial review is warranted where a choice exceeds legal or constitutional limits, has demonstrable adverse environmental implications, or is a clear abuse of power; an authority may engage in bona fide trial and error within its powers. The Court relied on Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal and referred to Ramana Dayanand Shetty v. International Airport Authority, Kasturilal Laxmi Reddy v. State of J & K, New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann, and Education Secretary v. Tameside B.C.

rule.if: is_appeal_challenging_municipal_project and project_serves_municipal_purpose and developer_finances_and_executes_project and council_receives_municipal_facilities and project_falls_within_council_powers and not clear_abuse_shown

predicates.is_appeal_challenging_municipal_project: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a municipal authority’s project decision.
predicates.project_serves_municipal_purpose: The project is intended to provide or improve facilities serving a municipal function.
predicates.developer_finances_and_executes_project: A private developer undertakes to finance and execute the project.
predicates.council_receives_municipal_facilities: The municipal authority is to receive facilities produced by the project.
predicates.project_falls_within_council_powers: The project is within the authority’s statutory powers.
predicates.clear_abuse_shown: The record demonstrates a clear abuse of power.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a municipal project that serves a municipal purpose, is privately financed and executed, provides facilities to the authority, and falls within its powers, the project method is not invalid merely because it is unconventional unless a clear abuse is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A municipal authority’s statutory power to establish markets and manage occupancy rights can accommodate a project in which a developer, with the authority’s consent, inducts occupiers into designated accommodation.
material_facts: The project included a vegetable market and commercial complex on municipal land.
The developer was to arrange occupancy of designated accommodation and retain premiums to meet the project’s financial outlays.
The Municipal Council consented to the developer inducting occupiers.
issues.conclusion: The exercise of power could be fitted within Section 272(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, and the provision did not need to be read restrictively to exclude the project.
issues.legal_principle: Section 272(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965, was capable of supporting the municipal authority’s exercise of power in this project. The Court declined to interpret that statutory power so restrictively as to exclude the enterprise.

predicates.is_appeal_challenging_municipal_project: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a municipal authority’s project decision.
predicates.project_establishes_municipal_market_fac: The project establishes or develops facilities for a municipal market.
predicates.developer_inducts_occupiers_with_council: The developer inducts occupiers into designated accommodation with the municipal authority’s consent.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a project developing municipal market facilities and the developer inducts occupiers with the authority’s consent, the occupancy arrangement can fall within the authority’s market-related power.

issues.legal_issue: A developer’s induction of occupiers into designated accommodation with the municipal authority’s express consent does not, without more, establish a prohibited lease or disposal of municipal property.
material_facts: The developer could arrange occupancy rights in the accommodation allocated to it under the project.
The Municipal Council expressly consented to the developer substituting occupiers in its place.
Occupiers, including those inducted by the developer, were to pay rent to the Council.
The appellants characterized the arrangement as a prohibited long-term lease, but the Court found that the essential elements establishing a violation had not been shown.
issues.conclusion: The essential elements of a transaction violating Section 92 of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act had not been established; the consensual substitution of occupiers was not impermissible.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 92 and 272(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965, should be applied according to their terms. A statutory power to establish markets and dispose of occupancy rights should not be burdened with restrictions absent from the statute. A developer’s substitution of an occupier in its place is permissible when done with the municipal authority’s express consent.

rule.if: is_appeal_challenging_municipal_project and developer_inducts_occupiers_with_council_consent and occupiers_pay_rent_to_council and no_prohibited_lease_elements_established

predicates.is_appeal_challenging_municipal_project: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a municipal authority’s project decision.
predicates.developer_inducts_occupiers_with_council: The developer inducts occupiers into designated accommodation with the municipal authority’s consent.
predicates.occupiers_pay_rent_to_council: The occupiers pay rent to the municipal authority.
predicates.no_prohibited_lease_elements_established: The evidence does not establish the essential elements of a transaction prohibited by the applicable restriction on disposal of municipal property.

issues.definition: When occupiers are inducted by a developer with the authority’s consent, pay rent to the authority, and the essential elements of a prohibited lease are not established, the arrangement is not a prohibited property disposal.

issues.legal_issue: A municipal project decision is not arbitrary merely because challengers allege that its estimates favor the developer, where the tender terms permit comparison and the record does not establish that the scheme was tailored to the developer or designed for unjust enrichment.
material_facts: The appellants alleged that the project estimates understated likely premiums from occupancy rights and thereby allowed the developer to make unjust gains.
Tenders were invited and five developers submitted tenders.
The tender terms allowed tenderers to identify the basis on which their offers would be compared.
No other tenderer expressed a grievance that the scheme had been tailored to the successful developer.
The Court found that the charge of arbitrariness was not made out.
issues.conclusion: The allegations that the scheme was tailored to the successful developer or afforded an unjust opportunity for enrichment did not establish arbitrariness.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 review of administrative action concerns whether power has been used properly or improperly; administrative-law reasonableness is context-dependent and is distinct from the reasonable-person test in tort law and the constitutional test for restrictions on fundamental rights. The Court referred to Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation, Nottinghamshire County Council v. Secretary of State for the Environment, Chief Constable v. Evans, and other authorities on administrative reasonableness.

rule.if: is_appeal_challenging_municipal_tender_decision and tenders_were_open_to_multiple_bidders and comparison_parameters_were_identifiable and no_other_bidder_complained_of_tailoring and evidence_does_not_establish_unjust_enrichment

predicates.is_appeal_challenging_municipal_tender_d: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a municipal tender decision.
predicates.tenders_were_open_to_multiple_bidders: The authority invited and received tenders from multiple bidders.
predicates.comparison_parameters_were_identifiable: Tenderers could identify the terms used to compare their offers.
predicates.no_other_bidder_complained_of_tailoring: No other bidder complained that the tender scheme was tailored to the selected bidder.
predicates.evidence_does_not_establish_unjust_enric: The evidence does not establish that the arrangement provided an unjust enrichment to the selected bidder.

issues.definition: When a municipal tender is open to multiple bidders, its comparison terms are identifiable, no other bidder complains of tailoring, and unjust enrichment is not established, an allegation of favoritism alone does not establish arbitrariness.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of a public body’s contractual decision requires a public-law element in the decision under challenge.
material_facts: The challenged decision concerned a contract between a municipal authority and a private developer for financing and executing a project.
The appellants sought judicial review of the contractual arrangement.
The Court found that the material placed before it did not show the public-law element required to justify interference.
issues.conclusion: The material did not justify judicial interference with the contractual decision.
issues.legal_principle: Although judicial-review principles apply to the exercise of contractual powers by a government body, the scope of review has inherent limits. A public-law element must be shown in the contractual decision before judicial review is invoked under Article 226 of the Constitution.

predicates.is_judicial_review_of_public_body_contra: The proceeding seeks judicial review of a contract made by a public body.
predicates.public_body_exercised_contractual_power: The public body exercised a contractual power in making the challenged decision.
predicates.public_law_element_shown: The material shows a public-law element in the contractual decision.

issues.definition: When judicial review is sought of a public body’s contractual decision and no public-law element is shown, judicial interference is not justified.

issues.legal_issue: A municipal authority’s otherwise valid project decision cannot be condemned solely because a developer may engage in transactions involving unaccounted money.
material_facts: The appellants alleged that the developer might make gains through transactions involving unaccounted money.
The allegation concerned the developer’s possible conduct in transactions relating to the project, rather than an established defect in the authority’s decision.
issues.conclusion: The possibility that the developer might resort to transactions involving unaccounted money was not, by itself, a basis to condemn the municipal authority’s decision.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review of an authority’s decision must address a legally relevant defect in that decision; condemning an otherwise valid decision solely on speculation about the developer’s possible transactions would not be a proper judicial remedy.

predicates.is_appeal_challenging_municipal_project: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a municipal authority’s project decision.
predicates.authority_decision_is_otherwise_valid: The authority’s decision is otherwise valid on the grounds raised.
predicates.unaccounted_money_conduct_is_only_specul: The allegation of transactions involving unaccounted money is speculative rather than established.

issues.definition: When an otherwise valid municipal decision is challenged only by speculation that a developer may engage in transactions involving unaccounted money, that speculation alone does not invalidate the decision.
